summary: The paper proposes CDAS, an intervention-based steering method combining a novel Jensen-Shannon distribution-matching objective with the distributed interchange intervention (DII) protocol borrowed from DAS, enabling bi-directional steering. The conceptual framing (steering as causal-feature identification rather than external-policy imposition) is fresh, and the two safety case studies (refusal override and CoT-backdoor neutralization with strong utility preservation) are compelling. However, the headline general-purpose benchmark results are mixed-to-weak, statistical rigor is uneven (error bars only in one of three experiments), and the generality claim is under-supported by the model/benchmark coverage.
strengths: Genuinely novel perspective: reframing steering as distribution matching (JSD) plus causal-localization-style DII, rather than likelihood maximization or preference optimization, is intellectually interesting and could be built upon.

The safety case studies are the strongest contribution: CDAS overrides refusals and neutralizes a CoT backdoor while preserving benchmark utility and achieving the lowest KL divergence, whereas RePS degrades badly (e.g., -27% TruthfulQA on Llama-3.1-8B). This utility-vs-effectiveness tradeoff is a meaningful, practically relevant finding.

Exemplary calibration and honesty: the paper repeatedly and explicitly states CDAS does not always outperform baselines, is sensitive to intervention layer, and needs factor tuning for general steering. Limitations are candid rather than buried.
The DAS baseline (CDAS with the objective swapped to Lang.) provides a clean isolation of the objective's contribution in the case studies.

key_concerns.issue: Weak/mixed headline results undercut the significance claim. On AXBENCH, CDAS underperforms RePS and Lang. on Gemma-2-2B and only wins at one of two layers on Gemma-2-9B; the abstract itself concedes it 'may not always outperform.' The general-purpose steering contribution is therefore thin.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either strengthen the general-steering results (more models/layers, better factor curation) or reframe the paper explicitly around the safety/utility-preservation regime where CDAS clearly wins, and scope the significance claims accordingly.

key_concerns.issue: Uneven statistical rigor. Only Case Study 2 reports seeds (3 inits) and standard error (Figure 1). The AXBENCH main table (Table 1) and the refusal case study tables (Tables 2-3) report no variance/error bars, so it is impossible to tell whether differences (e.g., CDAS vs RePS on Llama-70B) are statistically real.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report seeds, error bars, and significance tests across all main tables, not just Figure 1.

key_concerns.issue: Generality is under-supported relative to the claim of 'general-purpose steering.' The benchmark uses only Gemma-2 (2B/9B); refusal uses 3 models; backdoor uses a single self-trained Llama-3.1-8B. This is a narrow base for the broad claims about model-scale benefits.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add model families beyond Gemma/Llama/Phi and report whether the 'benefits from scale' trend holds beyond the few points shown.

key_concerns.issue: No controlled ablation isolating the DII protocol from the JSD objective. DAS ablates the objective, but there is no experiment holding the objective fixed while swapping DII for addition/clamping interventions, so the individual value of DII is unquantified.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add an ablation applying the JSD objective with a standard addition/clamping intervention (no DII) to isolate DII's contribution.

key_concerns.issue: The 'tuning-free' advantage is only demonstrated in the safety case studies; for general-purpose steering the paper shows factor tuning is 'paramount,' which partially contradicts a central selling point.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Clarify in the abstract/intro that tuning-free operation is regime-dependent, and investigate why concept-eliciting instructions fail to induce sufficient factor magnitude.

questions_for_authors: Can you provide error bars / significance tests for Tables 1-3? Several of the highlighted 'best' results have small margins.
What is the effect of the DII protocol alone? I.e., JSD objective with a standard addition/clamping intervention rather than DII.

Why does CDAS require large tuned factors (beta > 1) for AXBENCH if the DII implicitly samples natural factors? Does this indicate the counterfactual source instructions do not activate the concept subspace strongly enough?
How sensitive are the case-study results to the grid-searched intervention layer, given the AXBENCH results show strong layer sensitivity?
For the backdoor study with a single self-trained model, how confident are you the results generalize beyond this specific poisoning recipe?
calibration_check: Claims are unusually well-scoped to the evidence — the paper repeatedly acknowledges CDAS does not always win and is layer/factor sensitive — which is a genuine strength, though it also signals limited significance.

significance.justification: Safety case studies (utility-preserving refusal override, backdoor neutralization) are meaningful, but weak/mixed general-benchmark results limit broader impact.

novelty.justification: The JSD distribution-matching objective and the application of DII to bi-directional steering constitute a genuinely new perspective, even if the components are adapted from GANs/distillation and DAS.

rigor.justification: The method is sound and the DAS baseline cleanly isolates the objective, but the claim-evidence link for generality and the missing DII-only ablation weaken correctness.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only Case Study 2 reports seeds and standard error; the main AXBENCH and refusal tables lack any variance reporting, so many claimed 'best' margins are unverifiable.

calibration_honesty.justification: Exceptionally honest: the paper foregrounds where CDAS fails, its layer sensitivity, and its tuning dependence, and provides a candid limitations section.

clarity.justification: The method is explained in adequate detail but with dense notation and heavy appendix dependence; the core JSD/DII construction requires effort to follow.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard conference structure (intro, related work, method, benchmark, case studies, conclusion) is followed at appropriate length.

reproducibility.justification: Models, datasets, augmentation procedure, and factor definitions are described, with hyperparameters largely deferred to appendices; reproducible in principle if appendices/links were present.

related_work.justification: Positioning against Lang., PO (BiPO/RePS), DAS, SAEs, and safety-probing work is fair and reasonably complete for the prose available.

figure_quality.justification: Tables and Figure 1 (with standard-error shading) support the claims, though several tables are dense and the main AXBENCH table lacks variance.

breadth_generality.justification: Coverage is narrow — Gemma-2 only on the benchmark, three models for refusal, one self-trained model for the backdoor — insufficient to support the broad 'general-purpose' and 'scale-benefit' claims.

overall_recommendation.justification: A conceptually interesting, honestly-reported method with strong safety case studies but weak general results and rigor gaps; borderline reject needing substantial added experiments.
